newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- U.S. retail sales to show mild pickup.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- U.S. retail sales to show mild pickup.

text.p: The June retail sales report that the U.S. Commerce Department will release on Tuesday is expected to show that consumer spending picked up mildly in June from earlier in the quarter, economists said.

Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that retail sales rose 0.2 percent in June after slipping 0.1 percent in May. With auto transactions excluded, retail sales are expected to be up 0.5 percent after edging down 0.1 percent in May.

"Autos looked weak in June but we had more respectable performances in general merchandise and in apparel stores," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "The restaurant category is also due for a rebound. It's been weak for a while.
"These areas are not expected to be robust, but they should show improvement from what we've had," he said.
Kim Rupert, senior economist at Standard & Poor's MMS, looks for a slightly lower than consensus flat June retail sales report with sales up 0.4 percent excluding autos.
"We think home furnishings sales and other moderate retail store gains should help to offset a negative impact from the auto sector," she said.
Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Securities, said the market is looking for some rebound in department store sales.
"That would be another piece of information suggesting a modest or moderate trend of consumer spending during the second quarter," he said.
But Flanagan said for the bond market to rally on the retail sales number, it would have to see "a flattish or even a negative performance."

Economists at I.D.E.A. look for a somewhat stronger than consensus 0.3 percent rise in retail sales, and an increase of 0.7 percent excluding auto transactions. They look for a "bounceback" in sales at food service establishments.

"Spending for services is really reported later in the personal consumption expenditures report while in the retail sales data you mainly get a picture of stores that sell products," said I.D.E.A. bond strategist Josh Stiles.

"So the retail sales report isn't the total retail sales picture for June, anyway," said Stiles. "But we're looking for a small bounce. The consumer is beginning to spend again in June and we expect the pace of spending to pick up in July or August or September," he said.
Revisions to previous months' sales data often affect the market's reaction to retail sales data, economists emphasized.

"There's always the risk of revisions to previous months," said Flanagan. "Sales were down in April and May and if there's a significant revision to the prior months' data, that could outweigh the influence of the June data," he said.

"The initial estimate on retail sales is from a soft sample so usually you see substantial revisions," said Stiles. "Revisions tend to approach where the consensus was originally so the May number could be revised up," he said.
